newsitem.title: LEBANON: Pope ends Lebanon visit with call for peace.
newsitem.headline: Pope ends Lebanon visit with call for peace.

text.p: Pope John Paul ended a triumphant visit to Lebanon on Sunday with renewed pleas for peace in the Middle East and for a fully independent, democratic Lebanon.

The pope, who was welcomed ecstatically during his 32-hour visit, also repeated his call for Moslem-Christian reconciliation, calling Lebanon an example of co-existence for the world and the Middle East.

"I urge the Lebanese to continue this way, giving the region and world an example of co-existence between cultures and religions, in a society where everyone and each different community is considered equal," he said in a farewell speech at Beirut airport.
The pope flew to Rome aboard a special flight of the Lebanese national carrier Middle East Airlines.

Earlier, more than 300,000 people attended the pope's open-air mass in the heart of war-torn Beirut as thousands more overflowed into the streets and tens of thousands cheered him as he drove to the city.

Vatican officials said the size and warmth of the welcome -- including a near mobbing on Saturday evening by young people chanting "John Paul Two, we love you" -- exceeded even the expectations of the local church.
"It was many more than had been expected. That was the bishops' impression," Vatican chief spokesman Joaquin Navarro-Valls told reporters.

John Paul called on the world community in his farewell speech to ensure that the sovereignty, autonomy and security of Middle East countries were guaranteed and the rights and wishes of their people respected.
The search for peace in the region should be pursued "with determination, courage and coherence," he added.

"I also hope that efforts are continued and intensified to maintain Lebanon's growth, its progress towards an ever more democratic society with completely independent institutions and the recognition of its frontiers," he said.

This appeared an oblique response to complaints by the Christian minority that civil and political liberties have been restricted by pro-Syrian governments since the 1975-90 civil war from which the Christians emerged defeated and divided.

Asked why the pope's calls for Lebanese sovereignty during his visit did not specifically mention Syria which has 35,000 troops stationed in the country and Israel which occupies a southern border strip, Navarro-Valls said: "It is not needed."
"In three speeches he (the pope) has strongly and clearly expressed the need for a sovereign state," he said.

The pope told the Lebanese at Sunday's mass on a seafront esplanade in the war-ravaged heart of Beirut that their sufferings in recent years had not been in vain. "They will strengthen your freedom and unity," he said.
The message was reinforced in a 200-page papal document on the future of Lebanon which was published at the end of the service and expanded on the pope's theme.
Stressing reconciliation rather than recrimination, it was carefully worded to avoid stoking Moslem-Christian tensions and spare offence to Lebanon's powerful neighbours.
The document refrained from mentioning Syria or Israel, or echoing the blunt call for their withdrawal that Lebanon's bishops made in their conclusions to a Vatican synod held in 1995.
But the pope made the call for Syrian and Israeli withdrawal implicit in his document, saying Lebanon had to recover "total independence, complete sovereignty and unambiguous freedom."
